query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled laser shock peening (LSP) treatment to eutectic high‐entropy alloys with dual‐phase lamellar colonies will modify the internal phase boundaries—inducing compressive residual stresses and dynamically altering local dislocation structures—to reduce dislocation pile‐ups and delay microcrack nucleation. This single intervention should overcome the limited room‐temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing the alloy’s overall strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (for example, AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a hierarchical lamellar microstructure comprising ductile L12 (or FCC) and harder, brittle B2 phases that display semi‐coherent boundaries prone to dislocation pile‐ups.
generation.intervention: A single-step, controlled laser shock peening (LSP) process applied to the bulk alloy.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation tests under quasi-static and dynamic loading conditions; microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD for residual stress analysis) post-treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified internal phase boundaries that now carry compressive residual stresses and a more uniform, less pile‐up–prone dislocation distribution, thereby reducing local stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: LSP delivers ultrashort, high-pressure shock waves that produce localized plastic deformation near the phase boundaries. This process relaxes pre-existing dislocation pile-ups and introduces beneficial compressive stresses at the lamellar interfaces. The altered dislocation structure at the boundaries reduces local stress concentration sites that would otherwise serve as crack initiation points during tensile deformation. At the same time, the retained or slightly refined lamellar architecture preserves second-phase strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the LSP-treated HEA is predicted to exhibit an increased room-temperature tensile ductility (with a target increase in elongation that may approach 25–30% versus the baseline of ~18% elongation) while maintaining or slightly increasing the yield and ultimate tensile strengths (e.g., yield strength in the range of ~1100–1400 MPa).
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA exhibits a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar structure with evidence of dislocation pile-ups at semi-coherent L12–B2 boundaries that lead to local stress concentrations, microcrack initiation, and premature brittle failure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects of LSP are expected to be most prominent under room-temperature tensile loading; the response under very high temperatures or extremely high strain rates remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: While studies (e.g., PMC6175879 and PMC5818523) have shown that the chemistry and structure of phase boundaries strongly influence dislocation dynamics and can promote catastrophic damage, applying LSP to deliberately modify these boundaries in EHEAs has not been demonstrated. It is uncertain whether the shock waves will interact with the ultrafine lamellar architecture without causing deleterious damage or over-peening. The extrapolation of LSP effects—common in steels and other alloys—to complex HEA lamellar microstructures remains to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical eutectic HEA samples. Subject one set to optimally parameterized LSP (e.g., controlled laser pulse energy, spot size, and overlapping pattern) while keeping a second set as an untreated control. Perform detailed microstructural analysis (TEM to assess dislocation densities near phase boundaries and XRD for residual stress measurement) before and after mechanical testing. Subsequently, conduct standardized room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure from tensile tests
Local dislocation density and distribution along the phase boundaries (via TEM)
Residual stress profiles near the lamellar interfaces (via XRD or wafer curvature methods)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the LSP-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility (e.g., less than a 15% increase in elongation compared to controls), or if microstructural analyses do not reveal a reduction in dislocation pile-up or a beneficial modification of phase boundary stresses, then the hypothesis that LSP mitigates dislocation-induced microcracking while preserving strength will be refuted.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. Bulk versus Microscale Fracture Mechanisms
cited_evidence.text: The bulk uniaxial tensile deformation of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA showed extensive plasticity in L12 phase and dislocation pile-up induced microcracks in the B2 phase, resulting in shear traces and fishbone-shaped crack marks. These microcracks eventually propagated along the B2–L12 phase boundaries. Another study on the same alloy demonstrated considerable necking in the L12 phase and several fracture modes in the B2 phase, including shear rib, cleavage, and tongue pattern [,,]. The high strength of the B2 phase resulted in an overall increase in the strength of the alloy, and the back stresses resulted in a good strength–ductility combination. However, in this study, notched cantilever bending of the B2 phase showed quasi-cleavage mode of fracture. In bulk deformation, various extrinsic processes may constrain crack propagation. However, the absence of extrinsic mechanisms in the small-scale resulted in catastrophic failure of the B2 phase. Hence, quantifying phase-specific deformation mechanisms may aid in the design of the microstructure, such as the size and distribution of phases to achieve synergistic contribution. While the mechanisms responsible for this rather interesting behavior of Fe3Al have not been investigated in-depth, the simultaneous increase in strength and ductility of the cryo-rolled and annealed material with hierarchical microstructure composed of ultrafine recrystallized, recovered and partially recrystallized phases is evidently in excellent agreement,. In summary, the effect of thermo-mechanical processing by cryo-rolling and annealing on microstructure and properties of nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA was investigated. The cryo-rolled and annealed EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure after annealing. The synergistic effect exerted by the hierarchical microstructure resulted in outstanding increase in strength without loss of ductility when compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. The properties of many metallic alloys are essentially related to the structure, morphology and chemical distribution of boundaries. In terms of atomic structure, the phase boundaries contained in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were supposed to be insufficient in prohibiting dislocations due to their semi-coherent nature, which is similar to those widely reported in NiAl dual-phase intermetallic alloys,. However, in-situ deformation tests revealed that dense dislocation storage can be achieved within FCC phases and dislocation walls were formed along phase boundaries. The unexpected strong interfaces are thought to be highly related to the chemically disordered distribution of multiple solution atoms at phase boundaries as well as in the matrix of HEAs. Particularly, an ultra-thin segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width (Fig. 3b and S4), was detected near the phase boundary without forming complex intermetallic compounds, which were intrinsically brittle and would lead to stress concentration.
